こどもに最適な養育環境を 大阪府社協児童部会が中司こども政策担当大臣に要望
2026年11月25日 福祉新聞編集部大阪府社会福祉協議会児童施設部会（永野良子部会長）は１６日、中司宏こども政策担当大臣に対し、乳児院や児童養護施設の役割を再評価することなどを求める要望書を提出した。里親等委託率の目標が先行し、現場の実態との乖離があるとして、一人ひとりに最適な養育環境を選択できる制度を訴えた。
政府は２０１６年の改正児童福祉法で、社会的養護における家庭養育優先原則を明記。これを踏まえ里親などへの委託率について、２９年度までに乳幼児で７５％以上、小学生以降で５０％以上とする目標を掲げている。
同部会によると、社会的養護のもとで暮らすこどもの中には、発達障害や虐待によるトラウマなどで専門的な支援が必要なケースが多い。一方で、里親家庭の孤立や委託後の不調、施設への措置変更などの実態は明らかになっていない。
このため要望書は、委託率だけを追求するのではなく、こどもの育ちの質や長期的な成果を検証する必要があると指摘。専門性を持つ職員が２４時間体制でこどもを支える施設機能について客観的に評価するよう求めた。
また高いケアニーズを持つこどもが集中する大阪では、一時保護所や児童相談所がひっ迫しているという。現状のまま施設の小規模化が進めば緊急保護の受け皿が不足するとして、必要な施設機能や人員、財源を確保するよう要請している。
同日、永野部会長は中司大臣に要望書を提出。中司大臣は「二者択一ではなく、こども中心に考えることは大事だ」などと理解を示したという。
提出後、永野部会長は「施設を守り、里親を否定するわけではない。それぞれの役割や機能を尊重し合う『日本型社会的養護』に向けた建設的な議論こそが必要だ」と語った。

content:
Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
24th November 2026
I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months.
Here’s the video of the talk. In this post I’m going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply.
Coding agents in November 2025
Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5. With hindsight, this was a consequential model.
In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said:
Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach.
This held up.
Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025.
Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn’t been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn’t feel reliable enough—I had to correct it often enough that it didn’t feel like a clear accelerant.
The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right. It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself.
Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks.
The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work.
Fable class models in June/July
We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release, due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them.
In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5—a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work.
After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn’t get it back until July 1st.
For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models. My definition of these:
In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive, after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz
screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug.
A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm.
Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook.
I’d currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as “cheap Fable”). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well.
These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model.
3D modeling and game development in September/October
Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they’ll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for.
I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family. Here’s Gemini 4 Neon’s attempt at “Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data”, for example.
3D spatial awareness is crucial if you want to use vision LLMs for robotics. I don’t know if 3D modeling capabilities are a side-effect of the labs focusing on that or vice-versa.
Back in August I experimented with having Fable 5 build me a raccoon heist game. It had 3D graphics, looked like a game, and played really poorly. GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra did a much better job but the game itself was still pretty dull after the first 90 seconds of play.
I was somewhat relieved that designing a game that was fun appeared to remain a uniquely human pursuit. I even used that in a talk in September to reassure people that us humans still had a role to play!
Then, I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 “This game isn’t fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun.” And it worked. My Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay.
Opus 5.5 was the first model I’d used that appeared to understand fun. I’ve since worked on several little game projects where prompts like “Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful” produced results that kept me engaged for significant amounts of time.
Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026. I’ve been to two different conferences since then where people showed me game projects they’d been working on that really did feel like proper, worthwhile games.
The indie games scene has descended into a full-blown culture war over AI-assisted programming. A lot of people are calling GTA VI the last pre-generative AI blockbuster.
It feels like another inflection point to me.
Is Fable 5.2 an inflection point too?
I’m still trying to decide if Fable 5.2 represents a new inflection point, or just another incremental improvement.
I’m getting so much done with that model right now!
It seems to have taste that almost exactly matches my own. I have been burning through all sorts of gnarly problems that I’ve been thinking about (or procrastinating on) for several years now. The release notes for Datasette 1.0a42, 1.0a43, and 1.0a44—plus LLM 0.37, 0.37.1, 0.37.2, 0.37.3, and 0.38—all in the last three weeks, represent a flood of fixes, features and improvements.
If this does represent an inflection point, the key feature seems to be that if you can imagine and then clearly describe a piece of software, Fable can build it. That’s a wild thing to say, but it matches my experience over the past few weeks.
Software development has transformed beyond recognition in the last year. I don’t think I’ll ever go back to typing most of my code by hand.

title: Affordable Senior Housing Operator Embrace Living Communities in Growth Mode, With Acquisitions, Renovations Planned
description: Nonprofit senior living provider Embrace Living Communities is continuing on its mission to provide affordable senior housing to older adults through new growth via acquisitions and renovation projects. The Chicago-based provider operates 30 affordable communities for older adults and people with disabilities spanning 2,100 units, owning and operating 28 communities and serving as property manager […] The post Affordable Senior Housing Operator Embrace Living Communities in Growth Mode, With Acq
content:
Nonprofit senior living provider Embrace Living Communities is continuing on its mission to provide affordable senior housing to older adults through new growth via acquisitions and renovation projects.
The Chicago-based provider operates 30 affordable communities for older adults and people with disabilities spanning 2,100 units, owning and operating 28 communities and serving as property manager for two. Its portfolio includes 11 communities in Chicago, with 25 total in Illinois, three in Florida and two in Missouri.
Embrace Living Communities recently became the property manager for a community in Tinley Park, Illinois, and is in the process of closing an acquisition in Woodstock, Illinois. The provider focuses on providing affordable living options for older adults and people with disabilities in communities ranging from 24 to 150 units.
“We’re continually looking at properties,” CEO Wayne Foley told Senior Housing News. “We’ve got a few on our radar that we’re looking at, and we’re definitely in acquisition mode.”
The current environment for nonprofit, affordable senior housing providers is a “mixed bag” of both challenges and opportunities, with “a lot” of properties available for potential acquisition while factors like higher financing costs were making development more difficult, Foley said.
He described Embrace Living Communities’ approach to growth as conservative, and leaders evaluate opportunities on a regular basis to determine if future acquisitions could fit into the company’s existing portfolio.
“We say that we are a not-for-profit, but we’re also not for a loss and we don’t want to make a bad deal,” Foley said. “You make too many bad deals, you cannot continue operating.”
The organization looks for acquisitions within or near markets where it has an established presence. Embrace Living Communities properties are all independent living communities with activities and services available to residents, something Foley said was “very important” in providing quality senior living options for older adults.
“There are a lot of properties for sale, so I definitely see, you know, growth in our future,” Foley said.
This focus on growth stems from the fact that all the organization’s properties are maintaining extensive waiting lists, some of those waiting lists spanning “several years” as they “just keep getting bigger and bigger,” Foley added.
Interest rates and increased financing costs remain a barrier to funding significant growth, Foley noted. The nonprofit provider seeks state and federal funding when possible, but these avenues for public dollars have “limited resources” amid high competition for public aid.
The biggest challenge Foley sees rests in the lack of availability of affordable senior housing nationwide, noting that as a Section 8 housing provider, the organization is at the whim of state and federal funding allocations.
“Until money frees up or is allocated to that, we’re pretty much hamstrung, and we have to figure out a way to do more with less and bear the costs internally,” Foley said.
Affordability of senior living is a top issue for Foley, and he noted that the current gap between those able to afford private-pay senior living and those who must wait for access to subsidized affordable housing will only continue to grow.
Since 2022, Embrace Living Communities has completed four renovation projects encompassing 12 communities most in need of repositioning or rehabilitation. Another renovation project is planned, and if that effort is successful, Foley said he expects other opportunities to modernize and “freshen up” some of the organization’s older communities.
Renovation projects are “complete” overhauls of the communities, adding things like new flooring, cabinets and appliances while also updating common areas and shared spaces for residents.
Priorities for the organization include building up its financial reserves to cover future renovation projects while evaluating acquisition opportunities, Foley said.
“Residents love them and the residents have told us that they feel like they’re living in a brand-new community when we complete a renovation,” Foley added. “It’s more than cosmetic; we’re bringing it all up to date.”
Priorities in 2027 include focusing on improving staffing conditions and fostering better communication between communities, alongside evaluating cost-of-living wage increases and merit-based wage increases. A wave of retirements this year from the company’s original senior housing business, which was launched in 1980, is forcing leadership to find new staff to take their places in the organizational chart.
“Happier employees equals happier residents,” Foley said.
Looking ahead, Foley said he wants to see legislative action at both the state and federal levels to provide direct assistance, tax breaks or additional resources to affordable housing providers, with affordability shaping the coming years for the senior living sector, nonprofit and private-pay.
“I think the country is going to have to realize that something’s got to give here and give more help to this space,” Foley said.

title: ‘Like Foraging in the Woods’: Adaptive Reuse Still Challenging for Senior Living Operators
description: Adaptive reuse often is floated as an alternative option to make the most use of existing empty buildings. But operators can struggle to get these projects across the finish line to the point that some say it’s more challenging than building anew. Chicago-based Senior Lifestyle completed two adaptive reuse projects – the practice of turning […] The post ‘Like Foraging in the Woods’: Adaptive Reuse Still Challenging for Senior Living Operators appeared first on Senior Housing News .
content:
Adaptive reuse often is floated as an alternative option to make the most use of existing empty buildings. But operators can struggle to get these projects across the finish line to the point that some say it’s more challenging than building anew.
Chicago-based Senior Lifestyle completed two adaptive reuse projects – the practice of turning a different property type into senior living – between 2008 and 2015. The projects include a YMCA designed by architecture firm D.H. Burnham which opened in 1927 and a Catholic monastery on the northwest side of Chicago dating back to 1910. The company’s leaders used historic tax credits and low-income housing tax credits to offset the development costs, according to Robert Gawronski, vice president of development and acquisitions.
Today both communities stand as affordable senior living communities, with near-full occupancy.
But success as a senior living conversion is not guaranteed. Warrendale, Pennsylvania-based IntegraCare has signed on and pursued adaptive reuse projects, such as a hotel in a good location overlooking Chesapeake Bay, but never completed one yet. In the case of that project, issues during construction ballooned costs around 30% over budget. That pushed the operator to finish the project, but sell it to a new owner as a hotel when done.
“This will never be viable at senior housing, so we’re basically reselling it as a hotel,” Larry Rouvelas, CEO of IntegraCare, told Senior Housing News.
New ground up development averages $389,000 per unit, and backers of adaptive reuse projects can struggle with equal to greater costs and other challenges unique to the growth strategy.
‘Adaptive reuse often costs more’
Adaptive reuse projects are sometimes pitched as real estate plays where a buyer can get property for a good cost basis and then upgrade from there. Such projects have one glaring disadvantage compared to new development, though: costs.
Empty office buildings and hotels are targets for adaptive reuse, but the buildings may still resemble an office or school post-renovation. That can leave such projects less attractive in the eyes of prospects. Making matters worse, adaptive reuse projects can widely vary from one to another. A company might buy a hotel, for example, and find it has too-narrow hallways or restrictive layouts that affect how many units an operator can house when open.
“Adaptive reuse most often costs more than building from scratch, and you end up with not quite exactly what you were planning at a higher cost,” Gawronski told SHN. “From a market-rate perspective, it’s generally easier for people to go find a piece of dirt or to tear down an existing structure and build new.”
IntegraCare’s hotel conversion is in a good location with potential that rapidly declined once the operator and its partners opened up walls and began work, Rouvelas said. Cost overruns in wiring and plumbing “blew the project budget out of the water,” leading to a loss of millions of dollars and ultimately pushing the company to resell it as a hotel once renovations wrap up to recoup costs.
Office building layouts are often square-oriented with a large number of windows, which would leave a senior living common areas either too dim or “feeling cavernous,” Rouvelas said. Gawronski added these kinds of buildings often have floor plates that are difficult to meet the light and ventilation code requirements for residential units, resulting in deep rooms and common rooms without much natural light or ventilation.
Units in hotels are often smaller than what is found in senior living, resulting in “awkward depths” that struggle to be marketable to current seniors, who are pushing for larger units, according to Gawronski. Alternatively, there is the potential for a single loaded corridor approach, he added, but it results in inefficient layout for future staff.
Equity availability is going toward high end and luxury products, where margins are easier to gain after the cost of development and returns are often faster.
“The equity markets for development in senior housing have been stone cold for a long time,” Rouvelas said. “As the capital markets open up for development, it’s going to be for the most beautiful projects first. After that market gets overbuilt, that’s when people are going to be looking at alternatives.”
Location, location, location
For adaptive reuse projects that do work, location is important.
Senior living operator Vista Springs Living converted two closed elementary schools into luxury senior living communities in Grand Rapids, Michigan. The company converted classrooms and labs into studios and suites that are the “largest in the local market,” according to Founder and CEO Lou Andriotti. The property already had a commercial kitchen from which to prepare daily meals and outdoor playground space to turn into walking paths and exercise areas.
While plumbing was the biggest challenge to overcome, costs were between $50 and $80 per square foot cheaper than a new development, and one conversion qualified for greenfield tax credits to help offset the cost of the renovation. Spread over a 45,000 square-foot minimum project, it resulted in significant savings, more so when applicable tax credits are factored in, Andriotti said.
According to Andriotti, the location and quality of the schools made the projects viable from the start, but that’s not always going to be the case for other operators looking to attempt adaptive reuse.
“It’s like foraging in the woods for mushrooms,” Andriotti said. “These things aren’t easy to find … It’s not like every single one would have all the components.”
Despite the difficulties and losses with IntegraCare’s initial adaptive reuse project, Rouvelas still believes there is potential for the product type, but operators looking to tackle these projects need to be especially diligent when examining potential locations, from the wiring to the building makeup and how well it can conduct Wi-Fi in order to offer a modern senior living experience.
And for Senior Lifestyle, adaptive reuse is still on the table, but the project has to pencil in the first place, according to Gawronski.
“There has to be a situation where the building makes sense to convert for seniors in a way that’s marketable and functional, but also still on paper shows a pathway to a return on our investment for our capital partners,” Gawronski said. “If we find that, then it’s a win-win for everybody … We’re able to repurpose it so that it’s still contributing and serving that local community.”

title: 今年度のケアマネ試験、合格率が急上昇　27年ぶり40%台で歴代2位　合格者数は9年ぶり2万人超に＝速報値

content:
2026年11月24日
今年度のケアマネ試験、合格率が急上昇 27年ぶり40%台で歴代2位 合格者数は9年ぶり2万人超に＝速報値
10月11日に実施された今年度の介護支援専門員実務研修受講試験（第29回）の合格者が24日に発表された。【Joint編集部】
47都道府県の発表をJoint編集部が独自に集計したところ、受験した5万1602人のうち2万1520人が合格。合格率は41.7%にのぼり、前回の25.6%から16.1ポイントの急上昇となった（＊）。
＊ 集計は24日時点の速報値。今後変動する可能性もある。
受験者数は前回より1001人多く、3年ぶりに増加に転じた。合格率が大きく上がったことで、合格者数は前回から8559人、率にして66.0%増え、2017年度以来9年ぶりに2万人を超えた。
合格率が40%台に乗ったのは、1999年度の第2回の41.2%以来27年ぶり。今回の41.7%を上回るのは、1998年度に実施された第1回の44.1%だけだ。
都道府県別で最も高かったのは愛知県の49.2%。最も低かった青森県も29.9%となり、前回の全国の合格率を上回った。

content:
2026年11月24日
介護施設の嚥下調整食の提供を新たに評価 安全でおいしく、適切な栄養量を 厚労省提案｜来年度報酬改定
厚生労働省は20日、来年度の介護報酬改定に向けた協議を重ねている審議会（社会保障審議会・介護給付費分科会）で、特養や老健といった介護施設の「療養食加算」の見直しを取り上げた。【Joint編集部】
利用者の状態に応じて、安全でおいしく、適切な栄養量を備えた嚥下調整食を提供する取り組みを、新たに評価することを提案した。
現行の療養食加算は、主治医が発行した食事箋に基づき、管理栄養士や栄養士の管理のもとで、糖尿病食や腎臓病食、肝臓病食などを提供した場合に算定できる。
介護施設では既に、必要な利用者に嚥下調整食が提供されているのが現状だ。ただし、単に安全性だけに配慮したメニューを提供し続けることで、低栄養のリスクが高まるとの報告もある。
一方、厚労省の調査結果によると、嚥下調整食は常食と比べて提供コストがかさみやすく、栄養管理や食事ケア、ミールラウンドなどにかかる時間も増えると答えた施設が大半だった。
こうした嚥下調整食の質を報酬で評価する動きは、医療分野が先行した。今年度の診療報酬改定では、安全性やおいしさ、栄養量などに配慮した嚥下調整食の提供（＊）が、入院時の食事に関する「特別食加算」の対象に加えられた経緯がある。
＊ 一定の要件を満たすことも求められる。
今回の会合では委員から、介護報酬でも嚥下調整食の適切な提供を評価する案に賛同する声が上がった。また、食材費や調理の手間などを報酬へ十分に反映するよう求める意見も出た。
厚労省は今後、具体的な評価のあり方の検討をさらに進める考えだ。

content:
厚生労働省は20日、来年度の介護報酬改定に向けた協議を重ねている審議会（社会保障審議会・介護給付費分科会）で、居宅介護支援の「通院時情報連携加算」の見直しを取り上げた。【Joint編集部】
ケアマネジャーが利用者宅で訪問診療や往診に同席した場合も、評価の対象に加える案を示した。医療機関への通院時と同様に、利用者宅でも医療側との情報連携を促す狙いがある。
現行の「通院時情報連携加算」は、
● ケアマネジャーが病院や診療所での利用者の診察に同席する
● 医師・歯科医師らと必要な情報をやり取りし、お互いに共有する
● 医師・歯科医師らから提供された情報をケアプランに記録する
といった要件を満たせば算定できる。利用者1人につき月50単位。厚労省の調査（昨年度老健事業）では、「通院時情報連携加算」を算定していない事業所の12.5％が、その理由に在宅医らと利用者宅で連携していることをあげている。
厚労省はあわせて、既存の「緊急時等居宅カンファレンス加算」の要件を改め、ケアマネジャーのオンライン参加も評価の対象にすることを提案した。この加算は、利用者の急変時などにケアマネジャーが医師や看護師らと利用者宅を訪ね、今後の支援について協議・調整する取り組みなどを評価するものだ。
今回の会合では、こうした見直しが現場で医療・介護の機動的な連携を後押しするとして、早期の実現を促す声が上がった。厚労省は今後、来年度改定に向けて要件のディテールなどを詰めていく考えだ。

title: Senior Living Deals, Uneven Occupancy Gains and Slow Development Shape Second Half of 2026
description: Senior living transaction activity has reached a record high in 2026 as a narrow construction pipeline for new development puts more pressure on existing communities to meet demand. Affordability challenges and uneven occupancy gains also show that operators will need to rely on strong operations and not on demand alone to capitalize on growth. Transaction […] The post Senior Living Deals, Uneven Occupancy Gains and Slow Development Shape Second Half of 2026 appeared first on Senior Housing News
content:
Senior living transaction activity has reached a record high in 2026 as a narrow construction pipeline for new development puts more pressure on existing communities to meet demand.
Affordability challenges and uneven occupancy gains also show that operators will need to rely on strong operations and not on demand alone to capitalize on growth.
Transaction totals increased 13% this year, according to the Marcus and Millichap second-half 2026 national senior housing report. Deals priced at $10 million or greater led to this increase in deal activity as healthcare real estate investment trusts (REITs) continue to grow their senior housing operating portfolios (SHOP).
At the same time, fewer than 21,000 new units were under construction in the third quarter of 2026, roughly one-third of the nearly 61,000-unit peak that was recorded in 2019. Senior housing inventory jumped 0.9% in 2026 compared to last year, the report found.
These findings are a continuation of trends reported earlier in the year, with development challenges continuing to lead providers and capital partners to seek growth via acquisition. The latest report shows the operating environment may be getting more complex for providers with occupancy gains not translating evenly across all markets.
This uneven environment on occupancy comes as demographic-driven demand for senior living continues to rise, with the report noting that between 2026 and 2030, the population of people ages 80 to 84 is expected to grow by roughly 500,000 annually, a projection that is nearly double the previous average over the last 10 years.
That population growth is happening at a time when construction pipelines for independent living and assisted living have declined roughly 60% over the last five years, with the pullback on construction having the greatest impact on the memory care sector.
“Limited deliveries in these segments will leave existing communities to accommodate demand, making the competitiveness of their buildings and service offerings increasingly important,” the report’s authors wrote.
A short-term rebound of sweeping new development activity is unlikely. Challenges in financing new development have also grown following the Federal Reserve’s September interest rate increase and the 10-year Treasury bond yield eclipsing 5% as construction material costs continued to reach new highs in 2026, the report states.
These sustained development challenges have led providers to tackle bite-sized development with renovations and repositioning projects jumpstarting new growth, and the report’s authors cite these avenues for new growth as potential ways forward in difficult development conditions on a short-term basis. This push on renovations and repositioning projects comes as more than two in five existing senior living units are over 25 years old. But these efforts will not replace a broad return to new development and cannot keep pace with future new unit demand.
Occupancy rates have grown across the sector in 2026, but annual unit absorption varied by care type. This year, absorption of new units reached 3% of existing inventory for assisted living and 3.6% for independent living, compared to 0.1% for majority memory care properties and continuing care retirement communities (CCRCs).
Average CCRC occupancy in 2026 reached 92.3% while memory care occupancy was 88.2% in the third quarter, indicating that available capacity has not translated into stronger census growth, the report said.
“Outdated product, staffing limitations, and pricing constraints can make remaining vacancies harder to fill, potentially increasing the importance of targeted renovations and operating adjustments,” the report states.
The report’s findings suggest that the broader supply-demand imbalance will not benefit all providers equally and factors like building conditions, staffing capacity and pricing remain vital factors in converting demographic demand into move-ins.
Another constraint to how providers grow in 2027 and beyond is affordability, as senior living rental rates have increased 30% since 2021, with the largest increase in rental rates in independent living and assisted living. During the same period, multifamily apartment rental rates have increased by 20%, according to the report.
A common way older adults fund a move to senior living is through home or asset sales. While home price growth had slowed to 1.7% in August of 2026, the median price remained over 50% above its August of 2019 level. Also, the S&P 500 price index increased by 160%, the report states.
These gains in housing and equity values could provide a “financial cushion” for older adults using home-sale proceeds or assets.
“Limited supply could therefore strengthen property-level performance without meaningfully expanding financially accessible options,” the authors wrote.
The report suggests that affordability pressures could dampen rent growth and limit who can access senior living options compared to wealthier households. Currently open communities with “more attainable rates” could be better positioned to capture incoming demand and offer affordable living options.
Senior living providers and their capital partners continue to grow by new acquisition in 2026, and that trend is expected to continue in 2027.
In 2026, larger transaction sizes drove the record deal count as of June, and greater participation in senior living mergers and acquisitions (M&A) activity could further expand the buyer pool for stabilized communities and increase competition for newer assets with strong, established operators, the report states.
Deals below $10 million remained more than 60% of transactions, even as activity in that category held flat. The report’s sales data includes transactions of at least $1 million.
Smaller communities, those in need of renovations and turnaround opportunities could give private investors a chance at new growth. This comes as procedure changes for the Small Business Administration 7(a) and 504 lending structures now emphasize demonstrated operating performance, which could limit leverage for underperforming senior living properties whose buyers are relying on projected improvements.
“Stabilized communities with strong historical debt coverage should be well positioned, while buyers pursuing operational improvements may need more equity or alternative financing,” the authors wrote.
As new construction remains difficult, the condition, affordability and operating performance of existing communities will play an increasingly important role in how much of the coming demand for senior living the industry can meet.

Also, the S&P 500 price index increased by 160%, the report states. Senior living providers and their capital partners continue to grow by new acquisition in 2026, and that trend is expected to continue in 2027.

content:
Ladybird’s first alpha release
23rd November 2026
Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components—HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components—things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird’s even more ambitious predecessor project SerenityOS.
This morning the Ladybird project released their first alpha, which means you can now install the browser (on macOS or Linux) without having to compile it yourself!
I’ve been trying it out today, and it’s very impressive. It feels fast, the UI is lightweight and intuitive, and most of the websites I’ve tried to load in it have worked as they should. It looks like this (showing my video-compressor tool):
Here’s the process tree after I opened six tabs in one window and another tab in a second window (generated by this script, thanks Claude):
Ladybird (72925) [240 MB]
└── Hub (72926) [61 MB]
├── RequestServer (72927) [29 MB]
├── ProcessReaper (72928) [1 MB]
├── Compositor (72930) [123 MB]
├── RequestServer (72953) [36 MB]
├── WebContent (72984) [819 MB]
├── MediaServer (73006) [118 MB]
├── VideoDecoderServer (73007) [20 MB]
├── WebContent (73052) [144 MB]
├── WebContent (73057) [73 MB]
├── WebContent (73073) [166 MB]
├── WebContent (73094) [70 MB]
├── WebContent (73112) [116 MB]
├── RequestServer (73113) [27 MB]
└── WebContent (73185) [60 MB]
Ladybird runs different tabs in different processes, an isolation mechanism used by most browsers (well, technically Chrome uses a process-per-site).
I tried Ladybird against several of my more advanced tool examples—like the video-compressor shown above, which runs ffmpeg compiled to WebAssembly. I had it resize its own screenshot using my image-resize tool. It happily runs my Pyodide REPL (Python compiled to WebAssembly) too.
The one thing I tried that didn’t work was Datasette Lite, which runs Pyodide in a complicated arrangement of service workers and web workers. Attempting to start Datasette Lite displays this error:
undefined is not a function (evaluated from 'navigator.serviceWorker.startMessages')
I filed an issue about this, then found a FIXME annotation in the source code.
The October explosion
The project has been leaning heavily into coding agents this year. On February 23, 2026 Andreas Kling published Ladybird adopts Rust, with help from AI, describing how they ported parts of their LibJS JavaScript engine from C++ to 25,000 lines of Rust in two weeks using Claude Code and Codex.
Here’s the GitHub contributions chart for Ladybird over the past twelve months:
That uptick in October corresponds to the landing of a wealth of big improvements.
This Month in Ladybird — October 2026 describes what happened. In addition to moving style and layout to their own thread, landing a new JavaScript JIT, and replacing their C++ with Cranelift WebAssembly engine with new code that achieved a 7x boost on the JetStream 3 WASM benchmark, they gained 75,650 new passes on the ~2.25 million subtest web-platform-tests suite, beating Safari!
How did they do that? Coding agents:
Most of that gain came in five days, from about 2.12 million on October 22 to about 2.18 million on October 27. We pointed AI coding agents at WPT and asked them to fill in missing functionality. They made lots of small fixes, and those added up. Our biggest gains for the month were about 30,000 in
/css
and 10,000 in/editing
.
I’m interested in what models they are using here—I know Andreas uses Codex and Claude Code, but I haven’t seen him talk about specific model versions. Claude Opus 5.5 came out on September 22, 2026 and Claude Fable 5.2 on November 9, 2026 (after that window). I’d love to know what they were using for that huge leap in the last week of October.
Should you use Ladybird?
Here’s what Andreas says about Ladybird’s suitability for use as a daily browser:
This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details.
We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird!
Given how hard it is to secure a web browser, and the hostility of the environment they operate in, I won’t be using Ladybird to sign into GitHub or Gmail or any of my other sensitive accounts.
I’m going to keep it around for anonymous browsing though, partly to participate in the testing efforts but mainly because it gives me a glimmer of optimism to see a promising new entrant in the stagnant browser engine market start to grow its wings.

〈論説〉大腸がん体験記 検便からダビンチへ
2026年11月22日 福祉新聞編集部この夏も東京都杉並区の健康診断で検便をかかりつけ医に提出した。
「陽性反応あり」と呼び出され、大腸カメラ（内視鏡検査）実施の専門施設２カ所を紹介された。ＪＲ中央線阿佐ケ谷駅そばの河北総合病院を選び、大腸カメラを初めて受けた。
Ｓ状結腸がんを発見、推定３センチ、ステージⅡ。
昨年、新病棟が完成し、手術支援ロボット「ダビンチ」も導入され、「ぜひ」と頼んだ。米国産のダビンチは１９９９年登場、日本では２００９年承認、１２年前立腺がん切除を皮切りに保険適用が広がる。
入院１日半は絶食の上、手術室に運び込まれた。カニの足のようなロボットアームの下で、すぐ全身麻酔が効いた。５時間後、目覚めた時には完了。
その間、消化器外科医らは腹部５カ所に５～８ミリの穴を空け、カメラを挿入、１０倍以上に拡大可能なモニター画像を見ながら、アームを操作し腫瘍を中心に２０センチを切除、へその穴から抜き出した、という。
驚いたのは、下腹部に少し疼とう痛を感じる程度。穴は自然治癒、点滴棒を引きずりながらスタスタ歩けた。
手術支援ロボットは全国で約６００台、国産も登場したが、９割強は１台２～３億円のダビンチ、１カ所の穴で患部の切除可能な最新型も導入されている。
２週間で退院できた（病理検査でステージⅠに変更）。検便や診療所と病院の連携の大事さを体感した。
肛門に近い直腸と上部の結腸に悪性腫瘍が生じる「大腸がん」は、最新統計で年間の罹患約１５万４０００例、死亡約５万４４００人。がん死亡の部位別で女性１位、男性２位（日本対がん協会）。死亡率が欧米に比べ低下しない。
検便の陽性反応で大腸カメラなどの精密検査を受けた１０万６０００人のうち４４００人（約４％）に大腸がんが確認された（１７年、同協会）。大半は自覚症状のない４４００人もが死に至るリスクを抱えていた。
しかし、陽性反応が出ても精密検査の受診率は５～６割。厚生労働省は、まず検便の提出率を上げようと、２７年度から採便２回（２日）を効果がほぼ同じ１回へ切り替え作業を進める。
ところで、ダビンチ手術の値段は幾らか。
手術約９５万円、麻酔１４万円、検査・投薬などの包括６０万円、入院料１１万円など計１８５万円余。自己負担はその１～３割だが、高額療養費制度で例えば年収約３６０万円は入院・外来（世帯）の月額負担は上限６万１５００円で済む。一般や低収入者の負担を抑え、高収入層の負担は引き上げられた。
一方、ダビンチの維持費や、買い替え費用の捻出は診療報酬では難しい。手術回数を増やして加算金を得たり、入院期間の短縮でベッドの回転を早めたり、現場は四苦八苦している。
みやたけ・ごう 毎日新聞論説副委員長から埼玉県立大、目白大大学院の教授などを経て現職

2026年11月21日 福祉新聞編集部厚生労働省が１６日に公表した介護従事者処遇状況等調査の結果で、介護職員等処遇改善加算を取得している事業所で働く常勤介護職員の平均給与額は、２０２６年７月時点で約３４万９０００円だったことが分かった。前年同月から１万６０００円以上増加した。

title: 財政審、訪問・通所などの「集中提供型」を問題視　介護報酬の適正化を要請　来年度改定
description: 国の財政を議論する財務省の「財政制度等審議会」は20日、来年度予算案の編成に向けた意見書（建議）を片山さつき財務相へ提出した。【Joint編集部】 来年度の介護報酬改定をめぐっては、高齢者向け住宅の入居者らを主な対象とし […]
content:
国の財政を議論する財務省の「財政制度等審議会」は20日、来年度予算案の編成に向けた意見書（建議）を片山さつき財務相へ提出した。【Joint編集部】
来年度の介護報酬改定をめぐっては、高齢者向け住宅の入居者らを主な対象としてサービスを運営する「集中提供型」の事業所に照準を合わせ、報酬の適正化に踏み切るよう注文をつけた。
財政審がやり玉にあげたのは、高齢者向け住宅に併設・隣接する事業所だ。訪問介護・通所介護では、地域に点在する利用者を支えている「個別提供型」と比較して、同一建物減算が適用されている「集中提供型」の方が収支差率が高いと指摘した。
このうち訪問介護では、「集中提供型」の訪問回数や請求単位数の多さに言及。通所介護の「集中提供型」については、徒歩で事業所に来るなど送迎を伴わない利用者の割合が高く、基本報酬に織り込まれた送迎コストと実態にずれがあると問題視した。
財政審はこのほか、住宅型有料老人ホームの入居者を対象とするケアマネジメントの新類型「登録施設介護支援」にも言及。サービス提供の実態などを踏まえて、「報酬の適正化を行うべき」と求めた。

description: 厚生労働省は20日、来年度の介護報酬改定に向けた協議を重ねている審議会（社会保障審議会・介護給付費分科会）で、介護施設と協力医療機関の連携を推進する方策を俎上に載せた。【Joint編集部】 要件を満たす協力医療機関を定め […]
content:
厚生労働省は20日、来年度の介護報酬改定に向けた協議を重ねている審議会（社会保障審議会・介護給付費分科会）で、介護施設と協力医療機関の連携を推進する方策を俎上に載せた。【Joint編集部】
要件を満たす協力医療機関を定めるという介護施設の義務について、来年3月末までの経過措置を延長しないことを提案。一定の準備期間を設けたうえで、要件を満たす協力医療機関を定めていない施設に減算を適用してはどうかと投げかけた。対象は特養、地域密着型特養、老健、介護医療院。
厚労省はあわせて、一定の条件を満たせば減算の適用を猶予する案も提示。単独では協力医療機関の確保が難しく、市町村が中心となって行う「在宅医療・介護連携推進事業」の協議の場などで、その確保に向けた議論を進めている介護施設を対象にしてはどうかと説明した。
協力医療機関に求められる要件は、

特養と老健では現在、国のガイドラインに沿った対応が看取り関連加算の算定要件に位置付けられている。
介護施設のうち、運営基準などで原則すべての入所者への対応が求められるのは、介護医療院のみ。厚労省はこれを改め、特養と老健にも介護医療院と同様の対応を求めてはどうかと投げかけた。

title: 障害福祉の情報公表、未報告の減算を厳格化　毎年の更新漏れも対象に　厚労省提案
description: 厚生労働省は20日、来年度の障害福祉サービス報酬改定に向けた協議を重ねている有識者会議（障害福祉報酬改定検討チーム）で、情報公表制度に基づく報告を行っていない事業所に対する報酬の減算を厳格化する案を示した。【Joint編 […]
content:
厚生労働省は20日、来年度の障害福祉サービス報酬改定に向けた協議を重ねている有識者会議（障害福祉報酬改定検討チーム）で、情報公表制度に基づく報告を行っていない事業所に対する報酬の減算を厳格化する案を示した。【Joint編集部】
毎年度の情報の更新を怠った事業所も減算の対象とするほか、サービス類型によって異なる減算率を引き上げて統一することなどを提案した。
厚労省は今回の会合で、減算ルールの見直しや減算を適用する際の判断基準の明確化など、次の対応案を提示した。
● サービス類型により5％、または10％となっている減算率を引き上げ、統一する。
● 事業所の指定更新や運営指導などで未報告が確認された場合、その時点で減算を適用する。
＊ 現行のQ&Aでは、自治体が報告を指導しても事業所が応じない場合などに適用する取り扱いとなっている。
● 事業開始時に加え、毎年度の更新状況も確認し、未対応の場合は減算を適用する。
● 自治体は、事業所ごとに毎年度の報告期限を過ぎた段階で報告状況を確認する。
● 報告期限を過ぎた事業所を、自治体が審査支払いシステムで把握できる仕組みなどを検討する。
● 事業所が円滑に報告できるよう、報告を支援するツールの作成を検討する。
情報公表制度は利用者が事業所を比較・検討し、自分のニーズに合った適切なサービスを選べるようにするための制度。事業所がサービス内容などを自治体に報告し、自治体がその情報を広く国民に公表する。
厚労省は今回の会合で、現行の減算の適用率が実態に即していないと問題を提起。ルールに沿った報告・更新を事業所に徹底してもらい、最新の情報が公表されている環境の整備につなげたい考えだ。

description: 厚生労働省は20日、来年度の障害福祉サービス報酬改定に向けた協議を重ねている有識者会議（障害福祉報酬改定検討チーム）で、全サービスの事業者の代表者に要件を新設する案を示した。【Joint編集部】 福祉事業に2年以上従事し […]

厚生労働省は20日、来年度の障害福祉サービス報酬改定に向けた協議を重ねている有識者会議（障害福祉報酬改定検討チーム）で、全サービスの事業者の代表者に要件を新設する案を示した。【Joint編集部】
福祉事業に2年以上従事した経験など、4つの要件のいずれかを満たすことを求めてはどうかと提起した。人材確保への影響も考慮し、2029年度からの施行を提案した。
現場を支える管理者らに加え、法人経営に責任を持つ代表者にも一定の資質を求めることで、サービスの質の底上げにつなげる狙いがある。
厚労省は今回の会合で、一部の事業者に法令遵守の意識の欠如、利用者への不適切な支援、組織ぐるみでの不正事案などがみられると問題を提起。「サービスの質の確保が極めて重要な課題となっている」との認識を示した。
厚労省が示した要件の案は次の4つだ。
● 社会福祉法第19条各号のいずれかに該当する人（社会福祉主事）
● 社会福祉事業（障害児の場合は児童福祉事業）に2年以上従事した人
● 保健医療サービスまたは福祉サービスを提供する事業の経営に2年以上携わった人
● これらと同等以上の能力があると認められる人
会合では有識者から、自治体が「同等以上の能力」をどう判断するのかを問う声があがった。厚労省はこれに対し、例えば障害のある人の家族で、ケアの経験がある人などを想定していると答えた。今後、代表者の要件をめぐる具体的な検討をさらに進める考えだ。

障害福祉の虚偽・誇大広告にメス 厚労省が具体例の明示を提案 「無料」「高工賃」、どんな表示が問題に？
厚生労働省は20日、来年度の障害福祉サービス報酬改定に向けた有識者会議（障害福祉報酬改定検討チーム）で、事業者によるサービスの広告の規制を取り上げた。【Joint編集部】
事業所の指定基準で禁止されている「虚偽・誇大広告」について、どのような広告がこれに該当するのか、具体例を明示することを提案した。
医療分野では既に、ガイドラインで不適切な広告の事例が具体的に示されている。一方で障害福祉分野では、現行の指定基準に「虚偽・誇大広告」を禁止する規定があるものの、運用の判断の目安となる具体例は示されていない。
厚労省は今回の会合で、次のように問題を提起した。
「障害者本位ではないサービスの提供が行われている事案が相次いで明らかとなり、十分に質が確保されていないサービスを提供する事業者も参入してきている中で、広告規制の実効性の担保が課題となっている」
そのうえで、不適切と考えられる広告として次の例をあげた。
▶ 虚偽広告
●「必ず就職できます」と謳う。
●「◯◯％の満足度」など、根拠や調査方法を示さずに数字だけを掲げる。
▶ 誇大広告
● 世帯所得に応じた利用者負担や教材費の実費などが生じるケースもあるのに、条件や対象範囲を示さず「0円で利用」「無料」とことさらに強調し、無条件で費用が一切かからないかのような印象を与える。
● 条件や対象範囲などを示さず「送迎無料」と強調し、希望すれば無条件に送迎を利用できるかのように見せる。
●「◯◯市の指定を受けた事業所です！」など、事業を行う際の前提となる指定をことさらに強調し、特別な指定を受けたかのように見せる。
●「◯◯は効果が高く、おすすめです」など、具体的な根拠を示さずに特定のサービスの有効性をことさらに強調する。
● 目標額を得ている利用者が少数で、平均工賃も目標額を大きく下回るにもかかわらず、実績や達成条件を示さず「高工賃（◯◯万円）も目指せます」などとことさらに強調する。
厚労省は今後、「虚偽・誇大広告」に対する規制の実効性を担保するため、具体的な検討をさらに進める考えだ。

title: 介護報酬改定、基本報酬を重点に引き上げを　自民議連が決議　賃上げ財源の確保も
description: 自民党の介護福祉議員連盟（会長・麻生太郎副総裁）は19日、来年度の介護報酬改定に向けた決議をまとめた。【Joint編集部】 基本報酬の引き上げを重点とするプラス改定と、介護従事者の賃上げに必要な財源の確保を政府・与党に求 […]
content:
2026年11月19日
介護報酬改定、基本報酬を重点に引き上げを 自民議連が決議 賃上げ財源の確保も
自民党の介護福祉議員連盟（会長・麻生太郎副総裁）は19日、来年度の介護報酬改定に向けた決議をまとめた。【Joint編集部】
基本報酬の引き上げを重点とするプラス改定と、介護従事者の賃上げに必要な財源の確保を政府・与党に求める。
会合では、基本報酬をしっかり引き上げるべきとの認識でおおむね一致。決議案を了承し、今後の取り扱いは麻生会長に一任した。
議連は今回、物価や賃金の上昇に介護報酬が追いついておらず、事業者の経営や人材の確保は依然として厳しいと指摘。介護従事者の賃上げが他産業のペースに及ばないことに加え、在宅系を中心に倒産が過去最多のペースで推移していることもあげた。
決議で求めた対応は次の2点だ。
● 基本報酬の引き上げを重点に、今後の物価や賃金の上昇の見通しを踏まえたプラス改定とすること
● 全産業の賃上げ率や引き上げ額を考慮し、介護従事者について遜色のない賃金の底上げが実現するだけの財源を確保すること
会合には厚生労働省の熊木正人老健局長らも出席。全国老人保健施設連盟、全国介護事業者連盟、全国老人福祉施設協議会、全国介護事業者協議会、介護人材政策研究会の5団体も参加し、それぞれ要望を伝えた。

content:
障害報酬に利用計画集中減算を提案 中立、公平性確保へ〈厚労省〉
2026年11月19日 福祉新聞編集部厚生労働省は５日の障害福祉報酬改定検討チームで、サービスや支援の利用計画を作る「計画相談支援」と「障害児相談支援」について、特定のサービス提供事業者の利用が一定割合を超える場合、基本報酬を減額する仕組みを創設することを提案した。
相談支援事業所が障害者らに特定の事業者の利用を過度に勧める事例が見られるためで、中立、公平性を確保する。
ただ、中山間地などでサービス事業所が少ない地域、医療的ケア児者や強度行動障害のある児者を支援する事業所など、正当な理由があれば対象外とする。委員は大筋で賛成し、障害者の状態像は多様なため、正当な理由の議論は丁寧に行うよう注文があった。
また、児童期から成人期への移行を切れ目なく支えるため、指定基準に原則、計画相談支援と障害児相談支援の両方の指定を受けて一体的に行うことを明記する。居住地に相談支援事業所が少なく、障害者らが自ら利用計画を作る（望まないセルフプラン）ケースを解消する狙いもある。
利用計画案を市町村に提出する際、求められた場合はアセスメント記録の提出を義務付けることも検討する。アセスメント結果が利用計画案にどう反映されているか把握できるようにするためで、現在、厚労省でアセスメント記録の標準様式や評価方法を整理しており、まとまり次第、周知する。
ほかに、社会福祉士や精神保健福祉士の相談支援専門員を一定数以上配置している場合や、特定の災害時に安否確認や避難所への誘導などを行った場合に、新たに評価する。相談支援員が相談支援専門員になるための相談支援業務の実務経験要件を、５年以上から２年以上に緩和する案も示した。

content:
Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide
17th November 2026
Datasette Lite is my port of the Datasette Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide. I’ve released a complete rewrite of Datasette Lite using service workers, and it’s now almost indistinguishable from the real server-side application.
You can now do all of the following, using a carefully crafted URL to lite.datasette.io:
- Load client-side Datasette to browse any SQLite database, JSON file, CSV file or SQL script
- Select a released version of Datasette to load from PyPI
- Load a specific commit, tag, or branch name from the Datasette GitHub repository
- Pick from over 100 versions of SQLite to use with Datasette
- Install additional Datasette plugins from PyPI or URLs to wheel files, including JavaScript visualization tools
The ability to load specific Datasette references, plugins, and SQLite versions makes this a fantastic tool for linking to demos of work-in-progress features or bug reproductions, without needing to spin up a full web server to serve that demo.
As an example, consider the following URL:
Follow that link and, after a short loading screen, you’ll find yourself on a page that looks like this:
That’s Datasette running the new datasette-maplibre plugin, loading up a database of GeoJSON shapes of countries and displaying both a combined map and individual boundary maps in a table.
Let’s break down that URL to see what it’s doing:
https://lite.datasette.io/
?install=datasette-maplibre
&url=https://.../demo.db
&metadata=https://.../metadata.yml
#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent
The ?install=datasette-maplibre
installs that additional plugin from PyPI. You can pass &install=...
as many times as you like to load more plugins.
&url=https://.../demo.db
loads that SQLite database from the provided URL. These URLs need to have open CORS headers—I host files like this in Gists, because they provide an easy way to get open CORS headers on a web-hosted file.
&metadata=https://.../metadata.yml
loads this metadata.yml file. The metadata file adds HTML descriptions to various tables, and to the Datasette homepage. Visit that homepage here for a guided tour of the other features of that plugin, all defined in the metadata file.
#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent
is a fragment hash that turns into a location within Datasette—here it’s loading the /demo/capitals_and_countries
SQL view, then appending another fragment hash to it (%23
is a URL-encoded #
) which tells the map plugin to zoom to a certain location and to set the color of the shapes on the map based on the continent
column in the data.
That URL is doing a lot of work! I wrote more about this trick for building URL-addressable software in URL-addressable Pyodide Python environments last year.
The full set of supported URL arguments is described in the Datasette Lite README.
I’ve already started using Datasette Lite as part of the Datasette development process. Here’s a recent issue describing a pagination bug—I posted a comment there demonstrating the old, broken behavior and the new fix using links to Datasette Lite:
Demo of the bug: https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a42&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score—click next and the second page is empty.
Here’s that same page with the bug fixed (running on 1.0a43): https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a43&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score
How this works, using service workers
Datasette Lite is not a new project. I launched the first version back in 2022, originally as a bit of a joke (running server-side apps in the browser is pretty funny) but one that quickly started proving its value.
The problem with that initial version is that it was a hack. It worked by running Datasette in a Pyodide web worker, simulating requests through that stack, then injecting the resulting HTML back into the top level page using innerHTML
.
This worked for basic Datasette, but meant that any feature that used JavaScript failed to work, because script tags in innerHTML
don’t execute, and the web worker tricks it used failed to load additional JavaScript or CSS files.
The new version takes a completely different approach based on Service Workers. These allow JavaScript to intercept HTTP requests for new pages and resources and serve them from client-side code instead.
Datasette Lite registers a service worker for the entire lite.datasette.io
domain. The parent page then creates an iframe that sends requests for Datasette pages to URLs that look like this:
/app/aa94e6851595/ # the homepage (HTML)
/app/aa94e6851595/data/places # a table page (HTML)
/app/aa94e6851595/-/static/navigation-search.js # (JavaScript)
/app/aa94e6851595/-/static/app.css # (CSS)
Those are regular Datasette URLs, but with a /app/aa94e6851595/
prefix. What’s that about?
The /app/<session>/
prefix is necessary because of multiple tabs.
Consider the URL above, which loads the demo instance with the datasette-maplibre
plugin. That URL defines a full, custom Datasette instance. You might have that one running in a tab, then one of my other demo links running in another.
The service worker for lite.datasette.io
is shared between all of those tabs. If it routed to a single instance of Datasette then every tab would share that underlying instance, no matter what plugins or other settings their URL attempted to configure.
Instead, the parent page generates a random session ID and uses it as a prefix for all of the subsequent hidden asset and page loads. The service worker can then use that session ID to route those requests back through the parent page to a web worker running a dedicated Datasette instance for that particular session.
(We still need a web worker because Pyodide in a service worker would not be able to maintain state beyond around 30 seconds, depending on the browser. There are a lot of moving parts here!)
I had Claude Fable 5.2 generate several SVG diagrams to help explain this. Here’s my favorite of those, now embedded in the Datasette Lite README:
This system started life back in May as an AI research spike generated using Claude Opus 4.8. It wasn’t until November (and Claude Fable 5.2) that I felt familiar enough with how it all works to confidently ship it to production!
Bonus feature: pick your version of SQLite
I added this feature last night as an off-shoot of investigating a potential bug in SQLite.
Datasette is meant to work against any released version of SQLite since 3.25 (released in September 2018). There have been 87 further releases since then.
Being able to fire up Datasette against a specific version of SQLite is really useful for demonstrating new SQLite features and debugging weird issues.
In the past I’ve used various tricks to get different SQLite versions running with Python on my Mac, but it’s not a trivial process.
WebAssembly is perfect for this. I can load up a custom SQLite build entirely in my browser, test it there, then discard it when I close my tab.
datasette/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels is my new repository which contains WebAssembly compiled Python wheels for pysqlite3 for 163 different SQLite versions. Each version gets a file with a name like this:
pysqlite3-0.6.2-3.54.1-cp314-cp314-pyemscripten_2026_0_wasm32.whl
That’s for SQLite 3.54.1, the most recent version.
Datasette Lite now takes a special ?sqlite=
URL parameter, which will accept a version number like 3.54.1
, resolve the path to the corresponding wheel file, then fetch that wheel and install it into the Pyodide environment and configure Datasette to use it.
Once I’d built the wheels, I decided to have Claude Fable 5.2 build me https://datasette.github.io/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels/?versions=3.54.1,3.54.0&sql=select+json_object(%27a%27%2C+(select+json_array(1%29%29%29)">this bonus tool for comparing a SQL query across any selected versions of SQLite. Here’s an example showing how select json_object('a', (select json_array(1)))
differs between SQLite 3.54.0 and 3.54.1:
This should work for every other Python app, too
Nothing about how Datasette Lite works is unique to Datasette. Almost any Python application should be able to pull the same trick—running entirely in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide, as a cheap way to provide preview environments, demonstrate features, and recreate bugs.
C and Rust extensions used to be a blocker for this kind of thing, but any good coding agent can compile those to Pyodide-compatible WebAssembly now. You can even publish them to PyPI as of PEP 783 in April 2026.
One catch is databases. SQLite is no problem at all, but running PostgreSQL or MySQL in WebAssembly, while possible, is still a path less trodden.
I’d love to see WebAssembly preview environments like these become a common pattern across the Python ecosystem.

content:
Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
9th November 2026
Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven’t unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping. The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn’t want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator, a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room.
Here’s what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while:
You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners—I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra.
The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn’t work particularly well, so I added a “Rough mode” where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds.
Once that’s set up, the devices all listen for the beep!
I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room—displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound.
Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the “Sounds located” log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click “This is the mystery beep” to mark them as such.
Once you’ve confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map.
The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced.
How it works
When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices, a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here’s that paper’s abstract:
We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting.
That sounded exactly like what we needed to build!
Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server.
When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep.
How I built it
I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here’s that shared starter session, which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository:
Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve
There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it
I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from
There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app
Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though?
That got me this problem.md file. As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file.
The research looked good, so I told it:
Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else
That got me to this point—most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet.
I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released, and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces.
I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening and make live changes to the software as it ran.
This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an installModule() method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients.
On some devices, web pages that listen on the microphone request user permission any time the page reloads. The hot-swap module mechanism meant that we could deploy new code without having to manually interact with each of the listening devices in turn.
From that point on my involvement was mainly to sit by the laptop chatting with Fable 5.2 about what was going on, and occasionally requesting new features. Here are some of the feature prompts I ran:
I think we need to make it so I can drag things around on the map in “rough mode”, where my job is just to put them roughly where they are, then switch out of rough mode and it attempts to get them accurate
This gave me the ability to drag listeners around the map.
what’s a good way for me to test this I wonder? Can we have it listen for claps, then I could clap and it could identify the location of the clap? [...]
Claps should use a different symbol on the map than beeps
That added the thing where any time I clapped it would show on the map as a different symbol from the beeps.
each symbol on the map should include a HH:MM:SS timestamp
That made it easier to spot which symbol likely reflected which real-world sound.
The log should show beeps and claps with their timestamps AND have a little play button which, when clicked, replays the recorded noise from each of the listeners in sequence (with clear text on screen showing which listener recorded which snippet) while temporarily turning off microphone recording while that replay plays
Now I could replay sounds, making it much easier to identify which recorded clip was the mysterious beep I was looking for.
There should be a button next to a recording for “This is the mystery beep” - then I can hit replay to see and then confirm it was the mystery beep if that’s the one I am looking for
Then the system can categorize noises in the future to see if they are likely that same mysterious beep and use that information to build a more accurate idea of where it is
At this point I was getting close—I had a solid idea of where the beep was coming from, but wouldn’t it be neat if I could reposition the listeners around that point to get an even finer location?
I want a feature for this, I don’t want to have to restart each listening device etc, I want to be able to click a “Reposition the devices” button which lets me switch into repositioning, then I click “Repositioned” and it puts me into Rough mode and asks me to roughly locate them, then I do that and click, then it starts up again. The previous session can be read-only viewed through the app.
And since I had one spare device, I then said:
add a feature where the map includes a spot that is a suggestion for a location that it would be useful to add a listener at - based on data collected so far
Giving Claude Code ears
I think the most interesting part of this project is that I demonstrated it’s possible to give Claude Code ears.
Claude doesn’t have native audio input (yet), but it can run JavaScript and Python code that can analyze audio captured by a microphone.
I told it to run a web server with WebSocket connections to multiple listening devices, then had it both run a WebAudio microphone on those devices and hook them up so they could be sent fresh JavaScript code to execute via that WebSocket.
Then I could pretty much leave Claude alone, hacking away at the problem, querying the audio logs, and reconfiguring its ears to help it solve the problem.
I’m reminded of a similar hack I heard about at GitHub Universe a few weeks ago, where Martin Woodward told me he had been debugging the GitHub Universe Badge computers by plugging them into a computer via USB-C and then pointing a webcam at their screen, so his coding agent could tell if updates were working correctly or not.
Figuring out ways to let coding agents perceive the world around them is a whole lot of fun.
